explanation:
## The loop, and why every line of it is forced

```cpp
std::size_t lowerBound(const std::vector<int>& v, int target)
{
    std::size_t lo{ 0 };
    std::size_t hi{ v.size() };
    while (lo < hi)
    {
        std::size_t mid{ lo + (hi - lo) / 2 };
        if (v[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;
        else                 hi = mid;
    }
    return lo;
}
```

Hold the invariant in mind:

```
indices < lo   : known v[i] <  target
indices >= hi  : known v[i] >= target
the answer is in [lo, hi)
```

**Initialisation.** `lo = 0` and `hi = n` make both statements true about empty
sets of indices, so the invariant holds before the first pass. That is why the
empty array needs no special case: `0 < 0` is false, the loop never runs, and
`0` is returned - correctly, since in an empty array there is no element not less
than the target, so the answer is `n`, which is 0.

**Maintenance.** Two cases, and each tells you exactly what to assign:

- `v[mid] < target` - then `mid` is not the answer, and neither is anything left
  of it, since the array is sorted. Everything up to and including `mid` is now
  "known less", so `lo = mid + 1`.
- `v[mid] >= target` - then `mid` **is** a candidate; it might be the first such
  index. So it must stay inside the range: `hi = mid`, not `mid - 1`.

That asymmetry - `mid + 1` on one side, `mid` on the other - is the whole
algorithm, and it is a direct consequence of `hi` being exclusive while `lo` is
inclusive. Guessing it is how people end up with searches that work on most
inputs.

**Termination.** Each pass strictly shrinks `hi - lo`, because `mid` is always in
`[lo, hi)` so `mid + 1 > lo` and `mid < hi`. The range cannot stall, so the loop
ends with `lo == hi` - one position, which by the invariant is the answer.

## Upper bound is one character

```cpp
if (v[mid] <= target) lo = mid + 1;      // <= instead of <
else                  hi = mid;
```

Now "known left" means `v[i] <= target`, so the position returned is the first
index whose value is **strictly greater**. Everything else about the proof is
unchanged.

And that is why the two functions together are more useful than either alone:

```
v:        1   4   4   4   7   9   9
index:    0   1   2   3   4   5   6
target 4:     ^lower=1        ^upper=4      count = 4 - 1 = 3
```

`lower` is where the run of 4s begins, `upper` is just past where it ends, and
the difference is how many there are. For an absent target the two coincide at
the insertion point, which is why `count` comes out 0 with no special case.

## The overflow in the midpoint

```cpp
std::size_t mid = (lo + hi) / 2;          // the famous bug
std::size_t mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;     // correct
```

The two forms are algebraically equal and differ when `lo + hi` does not fit in
the type. `hi - lo` is at most the range length and cannot overflow, so the
second form is safe for any valid `lo <= hi`.

This is not a hypothetical. Java's `Arrays.binarySearch` carried exactly this
bug for nine years, using `int` indices: it broke on arrays over 2^30 elements,
where `lo + hi` exceeded `Integer.MAX_VALUE` and went negative. Joshua Bloch
wrote it up in 2006 as "Nearly All Binary Searches and Mergesorts are Broken",
and the fix was this one line.

With `std::size_t` on a 64-bit platform you would need an array of 2^63 elements
to trigger it, so it cannot happen here. Write the safe form anyway - the same
code with `int` indices, or on a 32-bit build, is one array size away from being
wrong, and the safe version is not harder to read.

## Half-open, again

`[lo, hi)` is the same convention as `begin()`/`end()`, the same as the
palindrome walk, and for the same reasons:

- an empty range is `lo == hi` rather than a special value
- the length is `hi - lo` with no `+ 1`
- nothing is ever decremented below zero, so unsigned indices are safe
- "not found" is representable as `hi` itself, a position that exists but holds
  no element

Half of the off-by-one errors in index arithmetic come from mixing an inclusive
`hi` with code that assumes an exclusive one. Picking one convention and keeping
it is worth more than being clever.

## Why linear would fail here

The statement caps `n` and `q` at 200000 each. A linear scan is 200000 x 200000
= 4 x 10^10 comparisons, which is minutes, not seconds. Binary search is
`log2(200000)` which is about 18, so 200000 x 18 = 3.6 million - a few
milliseconds.

The hidden cases are small enough to check by hand, so the time limit is what
enforces the complexity. That is deliberate: a correct O(n) solution would pass
every visible case and fail on scale, which is exactly how the mistake shows up
in real life.

## What the library gives you

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
auto lb = std::lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), target);
auto ub = std::upper_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), target);
auto count = ub - lb;                                      // or std::equal_range
```

`std::equal_range` returns both bounds in one call and does slightly less work
than two separate searches. All three are O(log n) on a random-access iterator
and **O(n) on a `std::list`** - the number of comparisons is still logarithmic,
but stepping to the midpoint is linear when you cannot jump. A detail worth
knowing before you reach for binary search on a linked structure.

Python's equivalents are `bisect.bisect_left` and `bisect.bisect_right`, named
after which side of a run of equal values they land on - a clearer name than
lower and upper, arguably.
